title: Aristotle in the Coffee Shop
author: Daniel Goodman
summary: Affirming the consequent, a classic logical fallacy, pervades leadership discourse through conspiracy thinking and bulverism. Leaders often assume conclusions are proven simply because predicted outcomes occur, then interpret all subsequent evidence through that pre-established bias. Bulverism especially disguises itself as empathy while psychoanalyzing disagreement rather than engaging arguments substantively. Sound reasoning demands testing hypotheses rigorously by seeking counterexamples and those who defy expectations, treating people charitably first before character analysis.
points: Affirming the consequent: assuming a theory is correct because its predicted outcome occurred, even if other theories explain the same outcome
Conspiracy thinking and bulverism both trap leaders in circular reasoning where any outcome becomes proof of pre-existing belief
Bulverism hides flawed reasoning under the guise of empathy, psychoanalyzing why someone believes something instead of testing whether their belief is true
Once a psychological profile is assigned, every word, gesture, and clarification gets absorbed into the conspiracy the observer constructed
Unfalsifiable theories and tedious conversation partners signal leaders are reasoning poorly; sound leadership respects those who defy expectations
quotes: In formal logic, this is a classic case of affirming the consequent. The structure goes something like this: If P, then Q. Q is true. Therefore, P is true.
You must show that a man is wrong before you start explaining why he is wrong. Bulverism works by this rule: instead of engaging with the substance of an argument, we pre-assume the speaker is wrong.
Once that psychological profile is assigned, every word, every gesture, every attempt at clarification is absorbed into the conspiracy they themselves constructed.
When the outcome is taken as proof of the very theory it was meant to test, the reasoner begins chasing his own tail.” Archived from Mere Orthodoxy on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
